subject: Physics
practicalPaper: Paper 3 is a 2¾-hour practical test (alternative to practical for private candidates) of three questions, of which candidates answer any two, for 50 marks. Questions typically cover mechanics, heat, optics/waves and electricity: candidates take and tabulate readings, plot a graph, determine a slope or intercept, evaluate a physical constant and state precautions, then answer short related theory parts.

practicals.title: Using the vernier calipers and micrometer screw gauge
practicals.aim: To measure small lengths accurately with a vernier calipers (to 0.01 cm) and a micrometer screw gauge (to 0.01 mm), correct for zero error, and use the readings to find the volume of a small object.
materials: Small wooden cylinder (e.g. a cut broom handle or dowel)
safety: Close the micrometer with the ratchet only; forcing the thimble damages the screw.
Do not drop ball bearings on the floor where people walk.
procedure: Close the jaws of the vernier calipers fully and check whether the vernier zero coincides with the main-scale zero. Record any zero error with its sign.
Place the wooden cylinder between the outside jaws and close them gently until they just touch. Lock the screw.
Read the main scale just before the vernier zero (e.g. 2.3 cm), then find the vernier division that lines up exactly with a main-scale line (e.g. the 7th). Add 7 × 0.01 cm to give 2.37 cm.
Repeat the diameter measurement at three different places and orientations and find the mean.
For the micrometer, close the spindle onto the anvil with the ratchet and note the zero error (thimble reading when fully closed).
Place the ball bearing (or wire) between anvil and spindle, turn the ratchet until it clicks, then read the sleeve (whole and half millimetres) and the thimble division in line with the datum line.
Add sleeve and thimble readings, subtract the zero error, repeat at different orientations and average.
Use the mean diameter to calculate the volume of the sphere or the cross-sectional area of the wire.
practicals.expectedObservations: Only one vernier line coincides exactly with a main-scale line. Repeated micrometer readings of a good ball bearing agree to within 0.01 mm; wire diameters may vary slightly along its length.
practicals.dataAndCalculations: Vernier: main scale 2.3 cm, 7th vernier division coincides, zero error 0.00 cm → diameter = 2.3 + 0.07 = 2.37 cm. Micrometer: sleeve 5.5 mm, thimble 28 divisions (0.28 mm) → 5.78 mm; zero error +0.02 mm → corrected diameter d = 5.78 − 0.02 = 5.76 mm. Radius r = 2.88 mm = 0.288 cm. Volume of ball bearing V = (4/3)πr³ = (4/3) × 3.142 × 0.288³ = 0.100 cm³ (3 s.f.).
precautions: Corrected for zero error.
Used the ratchet so the object was not squeezed.
Took readings at several positions and found the mean.
Read scales with the eye perpendicular to avoid parallax.
sourcesOfError: Object not perfectly round or uniform.
commonMistakes: Adding the zero error instead of subtracting a positive zero error.
Forgetting the half-millimetre mark on the micrometer sleeve.
Reporting a vernier reading to the wrong number of decimal places (it should be to 0.01 cm).
examTips: Always state readings to the precision of the instrument: vernier to 2 d.p. in cm, micrometer to 2 d.p. in mm.
Show the sum "main scale + vernier/thimble" explicitly; examiners award marks for the method.
State the zero error and how it was corrected; it is a common precaution mark.

practicals.title: Determining g with a simple pendulum
practicals.topic: Period, frequency and amplitude of S.H.M.
practicals.aim: To investigate how the period T of a simple pendulum depends on its length l and hence determine the acceleration due to gravity g from a graph of T² against l.
apparatus: Split cork (or two thin wooden blocks)
materials: Light inextensible thread about 1.2 m long
Plasticine or masking tape to mark a fiducial point
safety: Clamp the retort stand firmly or weight its base so it does not topple.
Keep a clear space so the swinging bob does not hit anyone.
procedure: Tie the bob to the thread and clamp the thread between the two halves of a split cork held in the retort stand.
Adjust the thread so that the length l from the point of suspension to the centre of the bob is 0.30 m (measure to the top of the bob and add its radius).
Place a fiducial mark (a vertical pin or line) behind the rest position of the bob.
Displace the bob through a small angle (less than 10°) and release it so it swings in a vertical plane without spinning.
Start the stopwatch as the bob passes the fiducial mark and time 20 complete oscillations. Repeat and take the mean time t.
Calculate T = t/20 and T².
Repeat for l = 0.50, 0.70 and 0.90 m (and further lengths if time allows), recording in a table.
Plot T² (vertical axis) against l (horizontal axis), draw the best straight line and find its slope s. Then g = 4π²/s.
practicals.expectedObservations: The period increases as the length increases. T² against l gives a straight line passing through (or very close to) the origin.
precautions: Used a small angle of displacement.
Timed 20 oscillations and repeated the timing.
Measured the length to the centre of the bob.
Ensured the bob swung in a vertical plane and that the point of suspension was rigid (split cork).
Avoided parallax when reading the metre rule.
sourcesOfError: Reaction time in starting and stopping the stopwatch.
Large amplitude makes the motion only approximately simple harmonic.
Draughts (e.g. ceiling fan) disturbing the swing.
commonMistakes: Counting the first pass as "1" instead of "0".
Measuring l only to the top of the bob.
Plotting T instead of T² against l and still expecting a straight line.
Taking the slope from table values rather than from the best-fit line.
examTips: Tabulate l, t, T and T² with units in the column headings (e.g. T²/s²).
Choose graph scales that make the plot cover at least half of the graph sheet; marks are given for scale, axes, plotting and line.
Show the large triangle used for the slope on the graph.
Explain why many oscillations are timed: it reduces the effect of reaction-time error.

checkQuestions.q: If the slope of a T² against l graph is 4.00 s² m⁻¹, g is
Which change has (almost) no effect on the period of a simple pendulum?
options: Doubling the mass of the bob
Moving it to a place with larger g
checkQuestions.explanation: T = 2π√(l/g) does not depend on the mass of the bob.

checkQuestions.q: Why is the time for 20 oscillations measured rather than for one?
options: To make the bob swing faster
To reduce the effect of reaction-time error
Because the first oscillation is always wrong
checkQuestions.explanation: The fixed human reaction error becomes a smaller fraction of a longer measured time.

practicals.title: Hooke's law and the spring constant
practicals.aim: To verify Hooke's law for a helical spring and determine its spring constant k from a graph of extension against load.
apparatus: Pointer (pin or matchstick fixed with plasticine)
safety: Do not stretch the spring beyond its elastic limit.
Place a box or tray under the hanger in case masses fall; keep feet clear.
procedure: Hang the spring from the clamp and fix the vertical metre rule close to it. Attach a pointer to the bottom of the spring.
Record the pointer reading R₀ with no load (or with the hanger only).
Add a 50 g mass (load W = 0.50 N, taking g = 10 m s⁻²) and record the new pointer reading R.
Add masses in 50 g steps up to 250 g, recording R each time; then remove them one at a time and record again to check that the spring returns.
Calculate the extension e = R − R₀ for each load using the mean of loading and unloading readings.
Plot e (vertical) against W (horizontal), draw the best straight line and find the slope; k = 1/slope.
practicals.expectedObservations: Extension increases in equal steps for equal increases in load; the graph is a straight line through the origin, showing e ∝ W within the elastic limit. Unloading readings agree with loading readings.
precautions: Read the pointer with the eye level with it to avoid parallax.
Allowed the spring to come to rest before each reading.
Checked readings on unloading to confirm the elastic limit was not exceeded.
Ensured the metre rule was vertical.
sourcesOfError: Masses not exactly their nominal values.
commonMistakes: Plotting pointer readings instead of extensions.
Forcing the line through a bad point.
Forgetting to convert grams to newtons or cm to m before calculating k.
examTips: State Hooke's law precisely: extension is proportional to the applied force provided the elastic limit is not exceeded.
Give k with unit N m⁻¹.
Mention checking on unloading as evidence the elastic limit was not exceeded.

checkQuestions.explanation: Permanent deformation occurs beyond the elastic limit.

practicals.title: Oscillations of a loaded spring
practicals.topic: Period, frequency and amplitude of S.H.M.
practicals.aim: To investigate how the period of vertical oscillation of a loaded spring depends on the mass and hence determine the spring constant.
safety: Use small displacements so masses do not fly off the hanger.
Keep the stand stable on the bench.
procedure: Suspend the spring from the clamp and hang a total mass m = 0.10 kg on it.
Pull the mass down about 1–2 cm and release so it oscillates vertically without swinging sideways.
Time 10 complete oscillations using a fiducial mark at the rest position; repeat and find the mean time t.
Calculate T = t/10 and T².
Repeat for m = 0.20, 0.30 and 0.40 kg.
Plot T² against m and find the slope s; k = 4π²/s.
practicals.expectedObservations: The period increases with mass. T² against m is a straight line (passing near the origin; a small intercept may appear because of the spring's own mass).
precautions: Small amplitude, vertical oscillations only.
Timed many oscillations and repeated.
Allowed the motion to settle before starting the stopwatch.
sourcesOfError: Mass of the spring itself not included.
commonMistakes: Using T instead of T² for the linear graph.
Mixing grams and kilograms on the axis.
Counting half oscillations.
examTips: Quote T = 2π√(m/k) and rearrange to T² = (4π²/k)m before using the slope.
Label the axes with quantities and units, e.g. T²/s² and m/kg.

options: The spring has mass of its own
checkQuestions.explanation: Part of the spring's mass also oscillates, adding to the effective mass.

practicals.title: Principle of moments with a metre rule
practicals.aim: To verify the principle of moments and use it to determine an unknown mass.
safety: Keep masses low over the bench so they do not fall far.
procedure: Balance the metre rule alone on the knife edge and record the balance point G (its centre of gravity, about 50.0 cm).
Keep the pivot at G. Hang the 50 g mass at a distance d₁ from the pivot on one side, e.g. at the 30.0 cm mark (d₁ = 20.0 cm).
Hang the unknown mass M on the other side and slide it until the rule balances horizontally. Record its distance d₂ from the pivot.
Repeat for at least five different values of d₁.
Plot d₁ against d₂; the slope equals M/m, so M = m × slope. Also calculate M from each pair and average.
practicals.expectedObservations: For balance, the larger mass is always nearer the pivot. Clockwise moment equals anticlockwise moment; d₁ against d₂ is a straight line through the origin.
practicals.dataAndCalculations: m = 50 g at d₁ = 20.0 cm balances M at d₂ = 25.0 cm. Anticlockwise moment = clockwise moment: 50 × 20.0 = M × 25.0 → M = 1000/25.0 = 40 g. With a graph: d₁/cm = 8.0, 12.0, 16.0, 20.0, 24.0 and d₂/cm = 10.0, 15.0, 20.0, 25.0, 30.0 → slope d₁/d₂ = 0.80 = M/m, so M = 0.80 × 50 = 40 g.
precautions: Ensured the rule was horizontal (balanced) before each reading.
Thread loops kept thin and vertical so distances are measured to a definite line.
Avoided draughts.
Read positions with eye perpendicular to the scale.
sourcesOfError: Friction at the knife edge allowing a range of balance positions.
Thickness of thread loops making distances uncertain.
commonMistakes: Measuring distances from the zero end of the rule instead of from the pivot.
Ignoring the weight of the rule when the pivot is not at its centre of gravity.
examTips: State the principle: for a body in equilibrium, the sum of clockwise moments about any point equals the sum of anticlockwise moments about the same point.
Show the moment equation with values before solving.

practicals.title: Centre of gravity and mass of a metre rule
practicals.aim: To locate the centre of gravity of a metre rule and determine its mass using moments.
safety: Keep the hanging mass close to the bench.
procedure: Balance the rule alone on the knife edge and record the balance point G (centre of gravity).
Hang the 100 g mass at a fixed mark near one end (e.g. the 5.0 cm mark).
Move the rule over the knife edge until it balances horizontally and record the new pivot position P.
Repeat with the mass at two other marks (e.g. 10.0 cm and 15.0 cm).
Take moments about P: weight of mass × its distance from P = weight of rule × distance PG. Calculate the mass of the rule each time and average.
practicals.expectedObservations: The rule balances alone near the 50 cm mark. With the mass attached, the balance point shifts towards the mass.
practicals.dataAndCalculations: G = 50.0 cm. 100 g at 5.0 cm; balance at P = 28.0 cm. Distance of mass from P = 23.0 cm; distance PG = 22.0 cm. 100 × 23.0 = M × 22.0 → M = 2300/22.0 = 104.5 g ≈ 105 g.
precautions: Rule balanced horizontally each time.
Avoided parallax when reading positions.
Repeated with different positions and averaged.
commonMistakes: Assuming the centre of gravity is exactly at 50.0 cm without checking.
Using the distance from the zero end instead of from the pivot.
examTips: Draw a labelled force diagram showing the pivot, the weight of the rule acting at G and the hanging mass.
Note that the weight of the rule acts at its centre of gravity; this idea earns a mark.

practicals.title: Archimedes' principle: relative density of a solid and a liquid
practicals.aim: To verify Archimedes' principle and determine the relative density of a stone and of a liquid (salt solution) from apparent losses in weight.
materials: Stone or metal sinker tied with thread
safety: Wipe spills at once; wet floors are slippery.
procedure: Hang the stone from the spring balance and record its weight in air W₁.
Fill the eureka can with water to the spout. Lower the stone fully into the water (not touching the sides or bottom) and collect the displaced water in a weighed beaker.
Record the apparent weight in water W₂. The upthrust is W₁ − W₂.
Weigh the displaced water and compare with W₁ − W₂ (verifies Archimedes' principle).
Dry the stone and repeat in salt solution to get the apparent weight W₃.
Relative density of stone = W₁/(W₁ − W₂); relative density of liquid = (W₁ − W₃)/(W₁ − W₂).
practicals.expectedObservations: The stone appears lighter in water and even lighter in salt solution. The weight of water displaced equals the loss in weight of the stone.
practicals.dataAndCalculations: W₁ = 2.60 N, W₂ = 1.60 N, W₃ = 1.50 N. Upthrust in water = 1.00 N; weight of displaced water ≈ 1.00 N. RD of stone = 2.60/1.00 = 2.60. Upthrust in salt solution = 1.10 N, so RD of solution = 1.10/1.00 = 1.10 (density 1.10 × 10³ kg m⁻³).
precautions: Stone fully immersed and not touching the container.
Eureka can filled to the spout and allowed to stop dripping before use.
Stone dried before immersion in the second liquid.
Balance read at eye level.
sourcesOfError: Water clinging to the stone or beaker.
Air bubbles on the stone reducing apparent weight.
commonMistakes: Dividing by W₂ instead of by the loss in weight.
Allowing the stone to rest on the bottom of the can.
examTips: State Archimedes' principle fully: a body wholly or partially immersed in a fluid experiences an upthrust equal to the weight of fluid displaced.
Relative density has no unit — do not add one.

practicals.title: Law of flotation with a loaded test tube
practicals.aim: To show that a floating body displaces its own weight of fluid and to determine the density of water (or another liquid) from the depth of immersion of a loaded test tube.
apparatus: Flat-bottomed test tube (or glass tube sealed at one end)
materials: Lead shot or small metal washers
safety: Handle lead shot with care and wash hands afterwards.
Do not overload the tube so that it sinks and breaks.
procedure: Measure the external diameter of the tube and calculate its cross-sectional area A; weigh the empty tube with its paper scale.
Add 10 g of lead shot, float the tube upright in water and read the depth h at which it floats.
Increase the load in 10 g steps and record h each time.
Plot h against the added mass m and find the slope and intercept.
Use mass floating = ρAh: slope = 1/(ρA) so ρ = 1/(A × slope); the intercept gives the mass of the tube.
practicals.expectedObservations: The tube sinks deeper as load increases; h increases linearly with m. The weight of water displaced equals the total weight of the tube and load.
precautions: Tube floated upright without touching the sides.
Read the depth with eye level with the water surface (bottom of meniscus).
Load distributed evenly at the bottom of the tube.
sourcesOfError: Meniscus around the tube making h uncertain.
Tube base not flat, so the immersed volume is not exactly Ah.
commonMistakes: Using internal instead of external diameter for A.
Forgetting to include the mass of the tube.
examTips: State the law of flotation: a floating body displaces its own weight of the fluid in which it floats.
Explain the hydrometer as a direct application — a frequent theory follow-up.

practicals.title: Relative density of a liquid with a density bottle
practicals.aim: To determine the relative density of kerosene (or palm oil) using a density (specific gravity) bottle.
safety: Kerosene is flammable — no naked flames nearby.
Dispose of kerosene into the residue bottle, not the sink.
procedure: Weigh the clean, dry, empty density bottle with its stopper: m₁.
Fill it completely with water, insert the stopper so excess escapes through the capillary, wipe dry and weigh: m₂.
Empty, dry thoroughly (rinse with a little of the liquid), fill with kerosene, stopper, wipe and weigh: m₃.
RD = mass of liquid / mass of equal volume of water = (m₃ − m₁)/(m₂ − m₁).
practicals.expectedObservations: The bottle full of kerosene is lighter than when full of water; kerosene has RD less than 1.
practicals.dataAndCalculations: m₁ = 25.20 g, m₂ = 75.20 g, m₃ = 65.20 g. Mass of water = 50.00 g; mass of kerosene = 40.00 g. RD = 40.00/50.00 = 0.800; density = 0.800 × 1000 = 800 kg m⁻³.
precautions: Bottle completely dry before each filling.
Outside wiped dry before weighing.
No air bubbles trapped inside.
Same temperature for both liquids.
sourcesOfError: Liquid on the outside of the bottle.
commonMistakes: Forgetting to subtract the mass of the empty bottle.
Giving relative density a unit.
examTips: Write the formula in words before substituting.
Relate RD to density: density = RD × density of water (1000 kg m⁻³).

options: To let air in when weighing

checkQuestions.explanation: Excess liquid escapes so the volume is fixed.

practicals.title: Coefficient of static friction
practicals.aim: To determine the coefficient of static friction between a wooden block and a plane, using (a) a horizontal pull and (b) the angle of an inclined plane.
safety: Keep fingers clear when the block slips suddenly.
Support the raised plank firmly.
procedure: Weigh the block with the spring balance to get its normal reaction R (on a horizontal plane R = weight).
Place the block on the horizontal plank and pull horizontally with the spring balance, increasing the pull slowly. Record the force F just as the block starts to move (limiting friction).
Add masses on top of the block in steps and repeat, recording R and F each time.
Plot F against R; the slope gives μ.
Remove the masses, place the block on the plank and slowly raise one end until the block just begins to slide. Measure the angle θ; μ = tan θ.
practicals.expectedObservations: Limiting friction increases in proportion to the normal reaction. The block starts to slide at a fixed angle that does not depend on the load.
practicals.dataAndCalculations: R/N: 6.0, 8.0, 10.0, 12.0; F/N: 2.4, 3.2, 4.0, 4.9. Slope ≈ (4.9 − 2.4)/(12.0 − 6.0) = 0.42 (from the best line ≈ 0.40). Inclined plane: block slips at θ = 22°, so μ = tan 22° = 0.404. Both methods give μ ≈ 0.40.
precautions: Pulled horizontally and gradually.
Plank surface clean and dry.
Repeated each reading and averaged.
Raised the plank slowly.
sourcesOfError: Jerky pulling gives readings above the true limiting value.
commonMistakes: Reading the spring balance after the block is already sliding (that is kinetic friction).
Using sin θ instead of tan θ.
examTips: Define limiting friction and coefficient of static friction μ = F/R.
State two laws of solid friction; they appear frequently in Section B.

practicals.title: Terminal velocity of a ball bearing in a viscous liquid
practicals.aim: To observe terminal velocity of a steel ball falling through glycerine (or thick palm oil) and to compare the viscosity of liquids.
apparatus: Tall measuring cylinder (500 cm³ or 1000 cm³)
materials: Steel ball bearings of different sizes
safety: Wipe up spilt glycerine or oil immediately — it is very slippery.
procedure: Fill the cylinder with glycerine. Place one rubber band about 8 cm below the surface (to allow the ball to reach terminal velocity) and a second one 20.0 cm below the first.
Measure the diameter of a ball bearing with the micrometer.
Release the ball gently at the centre of the surface and time its fall between the two bands.
Repeat with the same ball size and average; then repeat with other sizes and with a different liquid.
Calculate the terminal velocity v = distance/time.
practicals.expectedObservations: The ball accelerates briefly, then falls at a steady (terminal) speed between the markers. Larger balls reach a higher terminal velocity; balls fall much faster in water than in glycerine.
practicals.dataAndCalculations: Distance between markers = 20.0 cm = 0.200 m; time = 20.0 s → v = 0.200/20.0 = 0.010 m s⁻¹. Extension (Stokes' law): η = 2r²(ρs − ρl)g/(9v) with r = 1.0 × 10⁻³ m, ρs = 7800 kg m⁻³, ρl = 1260 kg m⁻³, g = 9.81 m s⁻²: η = 2 × (1.0 × 10⁻³)² × 6540 × 9.81/(9 × 0.010) = 1.43 Pa s.
precautions: Upper marker placed well below the surface so the ball had reached terminal velocity.
Ball dropped along the axis of the cylinder, away from the walls.
Eye level with each marker when timing.
Temperature of the liquid kept constant.
sourcesOfError: Reaction time with a short fall.
commonMistakes: Timing from the surface, where the ball is still accelerating.
Using diameter instead of radius in Stokes' law.
examTips: Name the three forces on the falling ball (weight, upthrust, viscous drag) and state that at terminal velocity they balance.
Sketch the velocity–time graph rising to a constant value.

checkQuestions.q: At terminal velocity, the resultant force on the ball is
checkQuestions.explanation: Weight = upthrust + drag, so acceleration is zero.

practicals.title: Uniform acceleration of a ball rolling down an incline
practicals.aim: To show that a ball rolling from rest down a uniform incline has constant acceleration, by plotting distance s against t², and to determine the acceleration.
apparatus: Grooved wooden plank or curtain rail (about 2 m)
Wooden blocks to raise one end
materials: Chalk or masking tape for marks
safety: Catch the ball at the bottom so it does not roll off the bench.
procedure: Raise one end of the plank slightly (a small, fixed angle) and mark distances s = 0.40, 0.80, 1.20 and 1.60 m from a start line.
Place the stopping block at the first mark. Release the ball from rest at the start line and time it until it hits the block.
Repeat three times and average.
Repeat for the other distances.
Plot s against t²; the slope equals ½a, so a = 2 × slope.
practicals.expectedObservations: Time increases with distance but not proportionally; s against t² is a straight line through the origin, showing uniform acceleration.
precautions: Ball released from rest without pushing.
Angle of incline kept constant.
Each time repeated and averaged.
sourcesOfError: Ball not rolling in a straight line.
commonMistakes: Plotting s against t (a curve) and calling it linear.
Forgetting the ½ when getting a from the slope.
examTips: Quote s = ut + ½at² with u = 0.
In ticker-tape questions, remember each dot interval is 1/50 s for a 50 Hz timer.

practicals.title: Resultant of two forces (parallelogram of forces)
practicals.aim: To verify the parallelogram law of vector addition using three forces in equilibrium.
apparatus: Two pulleys clamped to the board
Slotted masses with hangers (or three spring balances on a horizontal table)
safety: Ensure the board is secure; masses may fall if threads snap.
procedure: Tie three threads to a small ring. Pass two over the pulleys and hang loads P and Q; hang a load W from the third thread.
Allow the system to settle at rest (the knot in equilibrium) and mark the lines of the three threads on the paper with pencil dots.
Remove the paper and draw the lines of action from the junction point.
Using a scale (e.g. 1 cm = 0.5 N), mark lengths for P and Q along their lines and complete the parallelogram.
Measure the diagonal (resultant R) and compare it in size and direction with the third force W, which should be equal and opposite.
practicals.expectedObservations: The diagonal of the parallelogram is vertical and its length represents a force equal to W (within experimental error).
practicals.dataAndCalculations: P = 3.0 N and Q = 4.0 N at 90° to each other. By calculation R = √(3.0² + 4.0²) = 5.0 N at tan⁻¹(3/4) = 36.9° to the 4.0 N force. Measured equilibrant W = 4.9 N, so the percentage difference = (5.0 − 4.9)/5.0 × 100 = 2%.
precautions: Pulleys free from friction.
Thread lines marked with well-separated dots.
A suitable large scale used for the drawing.
Knot allowed to settle without touching the board.
commonMistakes: Drawing the forces to different scales.
Measuring angles from the wrong line.
Forgetting that the equilibrant is opposite to the resultant.

practicals.title: Specific heat capacity of a metal by the method of mixtures
practicals.aim: To determine the specific heat capacity of a metal block by the method of mixtures.
apparatus: Copper calorimeter with stirrer and lagging (or polystyrene cup)
Beaker, tripod, wire gauze and Bunsen burner (or electric kettle)
materials: Metal block (e.g. iron or aluminium) with thread
safety: Handle boiling water and the hot block with tongs; boiling water scalds.
Keep the burner away from the thread and paper.
procedure: Weigh the empty calorimeter with stirrer (m_c), then with water about two-thirds full (to get the mass of water m_w).
Weigh the metal block (m) and suspend it in boiling water for several minutes so it reaches 100 °C (θ₁).
Record the initial temperature of the water in the calorimeter (θ₂).
Transfer the hot block quickly into the calorimeter water without splashing, cover, stir and record the highest steady temperature θ₃.
Heat lost by block = heat gained by water + calorimeter; solve for the specific heat capacity c of the metal.
practicals.expectedObservations: The water temperature rises and settles at a final value between the initial water temperature and 100 °C.
practicals.dataAndCalculations: Block m = 0.200 kg at 100.0 °C; water 0.100 kg at 28.0 °C; copper calorimeter 0.050 kg (c = 400 J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹); final temperature 40.0 °C. Heat gained = 0.100 × 4200 × 12.0 + 0.050 × 400 × 12.0 = 5040 + 240 = 5280 J. Heat lost = 0.200 × c × 60.0 = 12.0c. So c = 5280/12.0 = 440 J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹ (close to iron, 450 J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹).
precautions: Transferred the block quickly to reduce heat loss.
Lagged and covered the calorimeter.
Stirred before reading the final temperature.
Avoided splashing water out of the calorimeter.
Read the thermometer with the eye level with the mercury meniscus.
sourcesOfError: Heat lost to the surroundings during transfer.
Boiling water carried over on the block.
Thermometer not reading the true maximum.
commonMistakes: Leaving out the heat gained by the calorimeter.
Using the wrong temperature changes for the block and water.
Mixing grams with J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹.
examTips: Write the heat-balance equation in words first, then substitute.
Give the unit J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹ (or J kg⁻¹ °C⁻¹).
A good precaution answer is specific: "the calorimeter was lagged with cotton wool", not "heat loss was prevented".

precautions: Ice dried before adding so no water at 0 °C was added.
Used melting ice (already at 0 °C).
Stirred continuously; calorimeter lagged.
Started a few degrees above room temperature and finished a few degrees below, so heat gains and losses roughly cancel.
commonMistakes: Forgetting the heat needed to warm the melted ice from 0 °C to the final temperature.
Using the mass of ice before drying.

Thermometer bulb fully immersed and not touching the glass.
Readings taken at regular intervals.

Drawing straight lines point-to-point instead of a smooth curve.

practicals.title: Linear expansivity of a metal rod
practicals.aim: To determine the linear expansivity of a metal rod.
apparatus: Metal rod (brass or copper, about 60 cm) in a steam jacket

safety: Steam scalds — keep hands away from the steam outlet and direct the outlet away from people.

Place the rod in the jacket with one end fixed and the other touching the micrometer (or dial gauge); take the initial reading.

Used the ratchet of the micrometer to avoid over-tightening.
Rod fixed firmly at one end.
sourcesOfError: Rod not uniformly at steam temperature.
commonMistakes: Mixing mm and m in the same calculation without converting both.
Using final length instead of original length as l₀.
examTips: Give α with unit K⁻¹ (or °C⁻¹).

practicals.title: Laws of reflection with a plane mirror (pin method)
practicals.topic: Reflection of light at plane surfaces
practicals.aim: To verify the laws of reflection and locate the image in a plane mirror by the no-parallax method.

Do not look at the Sun or a bright lamp through lenses or prisms.
procedure: Pin a sheet of paper on the board, draw a straight line MM' and stand the reflecting surface of the mirror on it.
Draw a normal at a point O on MM' and draw an incident ray AO at angle i = 20° to the normal; fix two pins P₁ and P₂ on AO well apart.
Looking into the mirror from the other side, fix pins P₃ and P₄ so that they appear in line with the images of P₁ and P₂.
Remove the mirror and pins, join P₃P₄ to meet MM' at O and measure the angle of reflection r.
Repeat for i = 30°, 40°, 50° and 60° and tabulate i and r. Plot r against i.
practicals.expectedObservations: For every ray r = i, and the incident ray, reflected ray and normal lie in the plane of the paper. The graph of r against i is a straight line through the origin with slope 1.
precautions: Pins fixed vertically and well apart.
Viewed the bases of the pins/images to avoid parallax.
Line drawn along the reflecting (back silvered) surface of the mirror.
Sharp pencil used for thin lines.
sourcesOfError: Thickness of the mirror glass (reflection from the silvered back).
commonMistakes: Measuring angles from the mirror surface instead of from the normal.
Placing pins too close together.
examTips: Trace sheets are often attached to the answer booklet — label every ray, normal and angle clearly.

practicals.title: Focal length of a concave mirror

Plotting u against v and trying to read f directly.

practicals.topic: Refraction of light at plane surfaces

Plotting i against r (not linear) instead of sin i against sin r.
Giving n a unit.

Attach the traced paper and make sure all rays and normals are labelled — many marks are for the diagram.

practicals.aim: To determine the refractive index of glass (or water) using real and apparent depth.

Measure the apparent depth from the surface to the search pin position.

No-parallax method used carefully.
Measurements repeated and averaged.

Measuring the apparent depth from the bottom.

Prism outline traced carefully and not moved.
Smooth curve drawn through the points.

Using A instead of A/2 in the formula.

practicals.title: Verifying Ohm's law
practicals.aim: To investigate the relationship between the potential difference across a resistor and the current through it, and to determine its resistance.

Never connect an ammeter directly across a cell — it is a short circuit.

Close the key and adjust the rheostat so the ammeter reads I = 0.10 A. Record the voltmeter reading V.
Open the key. Repeat for I = 0.20, 0.30, 0.40 and 0.50 A.

precautions: Opened the key between readings to avoid heating the resistor.
Cleaned wire ends and tightened terminals.
Ammeter in series and voltmeter in parallel, with + terminals towards the positive of the supply.
Avoided parallax when reading meters; checked meter zero errors.
commonMistakes: Connecting the voltmeter across the resistor and ammeter together.

Key opened between readings.

practicals.aim: To determine the specific heat capacity of water by electrical heating and to relate electrical energy to heat produced.
apparatus: Lagged calorimeter or polystyrene cup with lid
safety: Use only a low-voltage heater; never place a mains heater in a calorimeter.
Switch on the heater only when it is fully immersed.
Hot water scalds.
procedure: Weigh 0.200 kg of water into the lagged calorimeter and record its initial temperature.
Immerse the heater, connect it with the ammeter in series and the voltmeter across it.
Switch on and start the stopwatch; record V and I (keep them steady).
Stir continuously; after 300 s switch off and record the highest temperature reached.
Electrical energy = VIt; heat gained = mcΔθ; calculate c.

Stirred continuously.
Heater fully immersed before switching on.
Recorded the highest temperature after switching off.

practicals.title: Plotting magnetic field lines and neutral points
practicals.aim: To plot the magnetic field lines around a bar magnet using a plotting compass and to locate the neutral points.
safety: Keep iron filings away from eyes; do not blow them.
Keep phones, keys and steel objects away from the board.
procedure: Place the paper on the board away from iron objects and mark the magnetic meridian using the compass alone.
Place the magnet on the paper with its N pole pointing geographic north (along the meridian) and draw its outline.
Put the compass near the N pole; mark dots at both ends of the needle. Move the compass so its tail is at the last dot and mark again; continue to the S pole.
Join the dots with a smooth curve and add arrows from N to S. Repeat from other starting points.
Find the points where the compass sets in any direction (neutral points) and measure their distance from the centre of the magnet.
practicals.expectedObservations: Lines leave the N pole and enter the S pole and never cross. With N pole pointing north, two neutral points appear on the east–west line (equatorial axis) through the centre of the magnet, where the magnet's field cancels the Earth's horizontal field.

Compass tapped gently to free the needle before marking.
Small compass used for fine plotting.

commonMistakes: Drawing lines that cross.
Missing arrows on field lines.
Placing neutral points on the wrong axis.

safety: The coil and cells get warm — close the key only briefly.

procedure: Wind 30 turns of insulated wire tightly on the nail and connect it in series with the ammeter, rheostat, key and cells.

Increase the turns to 60 at a fixed current and repeat.

Key opened between readings.
Turns wound in the same direction and tightly.

Winding some turns in opposite directions so fields cancel.

practicals.title: Electromagnetic induction with a coil and magnet
practicals.aim: To demonstrate that a changing magnetic flux induces an e.m.f. in a coil and to investigate the factors that affect its size and direction.
materials: Cardboard tube (former) if winding your own coil
safety: Do not drop magnets — they lose strength and may chip.
procedure: Connect the coil to the galvanometer.
Push the N pole of the magnet into the coil and note the size and direction of the deflection; hold it still inside and note the reading; pull it out.
Repeat faster, then with the S pole, then with two magnets together.
Repeat with a coil of more turns.
Record the observations in a table and state the factors affecting the induced e.m.f.

Magnet moved along the axis of the coil.
Galvanometer kept away from the magnet.

Confusing Faraday's law (size) with Lenz's law (direction).
